entries.narration: Let's start with what a cloud service actually is. You ask for capacity through an API, you pay for what you use while you use it, and you hand it back when you're done. That is the whole operating model, and everything in this course sits on top of it. On the left are three services the retail application could use. In each column the same four layers appear: the hardware, the operating system and runtime, the application, and the data. What changes is who runs each layer. With a Compute Engine virtual machine, Google runs the hardware, and the operating system is yours to patch and harden. With Cloud Run, Google also takes the operating system and the scaling, so you hand over a container image and its configuration. With BigQuery, Google runs the whole query engine, and you bring datasets and SQL. Google calls this shared responsibility, and the important word is shared. The line moves up as a service becomes more managed, but it never reaches the top. What the data is, who is allowed to reach it, and where it lives are decisions only you can make. And elasticity cuts both ways: capacity follows demand, and so does the bill. So before choosing any service, we need to know where it physically runs. That is next.

Every Google Cloud resource lives somewhere, and where it lives decides what it can survive. A Region is a geographic area. Here it's europe-west2, which is London. Inside a Region there are zones, and Google's own guidance is to treat each zone as a single failure domain. So the scene places each resource in the narrowest box that matches its scope. A virtual machine and its zonal disk are zonal: if zone a has a bad day, that machine has a bad day with it. A Cloud Run service is regional, so Google runs it across the Region's zones for you. A Cloud Storage bucket with the location E U is multi-regional, which means its data is kept in more than one Region. At the top are global resources, such as a VPC network or a global load balancer, which have no single location at all. Here is the trap. Global scope describes where a resource can be used, not what it can survive. A VPC network is global, but its subnets are regional, and if every subnet you use sits in London, your application fails with London. Spreading across zones protects you from losing a zone. Surviving the loss of a Region needs a second Region, and a plan for using it. So never infer resilience from a word like global. Each service documents its own failure boundary, and the design has to be checked against that. With the physical side placed, next we look at the logical side: who owns these resources.

Now the logical side. Google Cloud organises everything into a tree called the resource hierarchy, and the rule that makes it work is simple: every resource has exactly one parent. At the root is the organisation, here retail dot example, which is tied to the company's Cloud Identity or Google Workspace domain. Below it are folders. This company keeps production and non-production in separate folders, so that a policy set on production can't leak into a developer's experiment, and the reverse. Folders hold projects, and the project is the level you'll touch most. A project holds the actual resources, records which APIs are switched on, links to a billing account, and carries its own access policy. Under the production project sit the storefront on Cloud Run and the orders database on Cloud SQL. Access policies set high in the tree are inherited by everything beneath them, which is why the structure deserves thought before the first project exists. One clarification matters here. A project is an ownership and policy boundary, not a network boundary and not an availability boundary. Two projects can share one VPC network, and a single project can hold resources in many Regions. So a project tells you who may act and who pays. It doesn't tell you what's isolated, or what survives an outage. Speaking of who pays, that's the next section.

Every charge in Google Cloud lands on a Cloud Billing account. The billing account is its own resource, separate from the projects it pays for, and it holds the payment arrangement, whether that's a card or a monthly invoice. Projects link to it. The relationship runs one way: a project is linked to only one billing account at a time, but one billing account can pay for many projects. Here, one account pays for production, development and the analytics project. Creating that link is deliberately a two-sided act. You need permission on the project to change its billing, and permission on the billing account to attach things to it. That's what stops someone from quietly charging their project to the finance team's account. The billing account doesn't even have to belong to the same organisation as the projects it pays for. Below is a hypothetical ledger for one month. The figures are made up, but the shape is real: every line ties a cost back to a project, a service and the usage that caused it. That's why project structure matters for money as well as access, and it's why budgets and cost reports are set on the billing account and then narrowed to the projects you care about. Notice too that owning a project, deploying to it and paying for it can be three different people, and in a real company they usually are. One caution: if a project loses its billing link, its paid services stop, and some resources can be removed for good. Next, we make our first real call against a project.

Everything you do in Google Cloud is an API call. Clicking in the console, typing a gcloud command and applying Terraform all end up calling the same service APIs. And APIs are switched on per project. Until a project enables the Cloud Run API, every Cloud Run call against it fails, however much permission the caller holds. So the session on the left starts by setting the default project, then enables run dot google apis dot com. You can run this in Cloud Shell, a terminal in the browser with gcloud already installed and already signed in as you. Your home directory there keeps five gigabytes between sessions, but the machine behind it is temporary. The third command describes the project, and the output shows three different identifiers that are easy to confuse. The project ID, retail dev forty-eight twenty-one, is chosen when the project is created, is unique across all of Google Cloud, and can never change. The project number is assigned by Google, and many APIs use it internally. The display name is just a label for people, and you can edit it whenever you like. Finally, look at the full resource name at the bottom. It reads left to right: the service's API host, then the project, then the location, then the resource itself. You'll see that shape again in access policies and audit logs. Last in this chapter: keeping costs and clutter under control.

A budget watches spend on a billing account, or on part of one, and compares it with an amount you set. When spend crosses a threshold, by default fifty, ninety and a hundred percent, it sends an alert. The plot shows a hypothetical month for the development project. A traffic test starts on day eighteen, spend climbs faster, and the alerts fire at fifty, then ninety, then a hundred percent. Look at what the line does next. It keeps climbing. An alert-only budget notifies people. It doesn't stop anything, and the alert arrives after the spend has happened. Google does offer a separate spend-cap budget type that pauses one chosen service, but that's a distinct control you'd set up deliberately, and costs can still overrun before it takes effect. To find out where the money went, you need metadata on resources. Labels are key-value pairs on a single resource, such as team equals checkout, and they flow into cost reports. Tags are defined centrally, are inherited down the hierarchy, and can be used in access and organisation policy conditions. Finally, cleanup. You can delete the resources in a project, or shut the project down entirely. A shut-down project waits thirty days and can be restored in that window. Disable its billing first, because charges can keep accruing until the current billing cycle ends. After that, it's gone for good, and its project ID can never be used again. With ownership, location and cost in place, next we decide who is allowed to act at all.

Chapter one ended with a question: who is allowed to act? Before IAM can answer that, every request has to say who is asking. Google Cloud calls the asker a principal, meaning any identity that a policy can name. People usually have Google Accounts, managed by the company through Cloud Identity or Google Workspace, so alice at retail dot example is a principal. Groups are principals too, and they're the better place to grant access, because joining and leaving a team then changes access without anyone touching a policy. Workloads get service accounts, identities that belong to software rather than to a person. And if your people or your build systems already sign in somewhere else, an external identity provider can vouch for them through federation, so they never need a separate Google password or a stored key. There's also one special principal, all users, which means anyone on the internet, so granting a role to it makes something public. Now follow the band below them. A request arrives with a credential. Authentication checks that credential and answers one question only: who are you? Then authorisation, which is IAM, asks a separate question: does any policy allow this identity to perform this action on this resource? Keep those two apart. A perfectly valid sign-in grants no access at all. Many confusing errors make sense once you ask which of the two questions failed. Next, we look at how IAM policies actually grant access.

Here's what an allow policy looks like when you ask gcloud for it. It's a list of bindings, and each binding says: this role, for these members. The checkout developers' group gets Cloud Run Developer, so they can deploy and update services. The orders A P I service account gets Cloud SQL Client, so it can connect to the database instance. And the S R E group gets Viewer. A role, in turn, is just a named set of permissions, and each permission names a service, a resource type and a verb, such as run dot services dot get. Roles come in three kinds. The basic roles, Owner, Editor and Viewer, predate IAM's fine-grained model and each carry an enormous number of permissions across almost every service, so they're a poor fit for production. Predefined roles are written per service by Google and kept up to date as services change. Custom roles are your own lists of permissions, which also means keeping them current is your job. Policies attach to the organisation, to folders, to projects, and to many individual resources such as a bucket or a single Cloud Run service. Grant on the smallest resource that works: a role on one bucket is far easier to reason about than the same role on the whole project. What a principal can actually do is the union of the resource's own policy and every policy above it. So an allow policy can only ever add access. To take access away, you need something else, which is next.

If allow policies only add, how do you guarantee that something can't happen? Google gives IAM three kinds of policy, and its documentation describes them as stages. First, principal access boundary policies decide which resources a principal is eligible to use at all. Second, deny policies: if a deny rule matches the principal and the permission, the request is refused, no matter how many roles would have allowed it. Only then do allow policies matter, where some binding has to grant the permission. Look at the deny policy on the left. It denies project deletion to everyone, written as the public principal set, with one exception: the platform admins group. Notice the permission format is different from an allow policy. It's written with the service's full domain name, cloudresourcemanager dot google apis dot com, slash projects dot delete. A deny rule can carry its own condition too, but that condition can only test resource tags. Attached at the organisation, that rule reaches every folder and project beneath it. Conditions work differently. A condition belongs to a single allow binding and narrows it. The bottom card grants a contractor Cloud Run Developer, but only until the first of November, after which the binding simply stops applying. Conditions can also test resource tags, which you met in chapter one. So effective access is never one policy. It's boundaries, then denials, then grants. Next, the identities your workloads use.

When the retail application's code reads from the database, it shouldn't be doing so as Alice, or as anyone else. It runs as a service account, an identity that belongs to the workload. There are three kinds to tell apart. Your own service accounts, like orders A P I, are created by you, given exactly the roles their workload needs, and retired when the workload goes. Default service accounts are created automatically when you enable certain APIs. The Compute Engine default account, for example, can be granted the very broad Editor role on the project, unless an organisation policy stops that automatic grant. Newer organisations enforce that policy by default, but older ones often don't, so check. Service agents are different again. Google manages them, and a service uses its agent to act inside your project on your behalf, for example to pull a container image. Treat their grants as part of the service and change them with care. Now the subtle part. A service account has two faces. As a principal, it holds roles and makes calls. But it's also a resource, so other principals can hold roles on it, such as permission to attach it to a workload or to borrow its identity. Those grants are often the real security boundary. When retiring one, disable it first and watch for failures. A deleted one can be undeleted for thirty days. Next: how code actually gets credentials.

How does running code actually get a credential? Google's client libraries use Application Default Credentials, which looks in three places in a fixed order. First, an environment variable pointing at a credential file. Second, a file written when you run gcloud auth application default login on your own machine. Third, on Google Cloud, the service account attached to the workload, fetched as a short-lived token from the metadata server. That third path is the one production should use. Be clear about what ADC does: it finds a credential. It grants nothing. What that identity may do is still decided by IAM. Next, two different powers over a service account that are easy to confuse. Act as, from the Service Account User role, lets you attach the account to something you deploy, so the workload runs as it. Get access token, from the Token Creator role, lets you mint tokens and act as the account directly, which is impersonation. Either way, the permission to use an identity is separate from the permissions that identity holds, and both deserve review. Finally, workloads outside Google Cloud, such as a build pipeline. With workload identity federation, the job presents its own signed token, Google's Security Token Service checks it against rules you set, and returns a short-lived token. No key file ever exists, so none can leak. Next, the difference between managing a resource and reading its data.

Here's a failure you'll meet early. The orders A P I service account can be deployed, it runs, it connects to its database. Then it tries to read an export file from a Cloud Storage bucket, and gets a 403. Read the message carefully, because it tells you nearly everything. It names the principal, orders A P I. It names the missing permission, storage dot objects dot get. And it adds, or it may not exist. That phrase is deliberate. A refusal won't confirm whether the object is there, so someone without access learns nothing from probing. The fix isn't Owner or Editor. It's the narrowest role containing that permission, Storage Object Viewer, granted on that one bucket. The broader lesson is in the table. Being able to administer a resource and being able to read its data are different things, and each service draws the line in its own place. Cloud Run Admin manages services, but a service holds no data of its own. Cloud SQL Client lets you open a connection to an instance, but what you can read inside the database is decided by database users and grants, which IAM doesn't manage for you by default. BigQuery separates running a query job in a project from reading the dataset it touches, so you often need both. So when access fails, ask which side of that line you're on. Next, guard-rails on configuration itself.

So far every control has been about people and workloads. Organization Policy is about configuration. It doesn't ask who you are. It asks whether the thing you're trying to create or change is allowed at all. The card on the left sets the resource locations constraint on the whole organisation, allowing only the value group europe locations. Now a project Owner, whom IAM allows to do almost anything, tries to create a bucket in us-central1. The request is refused, because the constraint applies whoever asks. That's the difference between the two controls. IAM decides who may perform an action. Organization Policy decides what configuration is permitted. Constraints come in two broad shapes. List constraints allow or deny specific values, such as locations or which domains may appear in IAM policies. Boolean constraints turn a behaviour on or off, such as stopping anyone from creating service account keys. Like IAM, they're set on the organisation, a folder or a project, and are inherited downwards, with rules for how a lower level may change them. Organisations created since May twenty twenty-four start with a baseline of these enforced, including that key creation block. Older organisations may have none, so check rather than assume. And remember, a constraint never grants access. It only removes possibilities. Finally, putting it all together into a design.

Let's turn everything in this chapter into a plan you could review. The table is the retail company's role matrix: who holds what, in each environment. Developers deploy freely in development but can only view production. The S R E group can read logs and metrics in production without being able to change anything. The deployment pipeline's service account can deploy to production and can act as the orders A P I account, so new revisions run as that identity and nothing more. Auditors get the private log viewer role, which is what reading Data Access logs requires. And orders A P I itself holds only what the running service needs: a database connection and one secret. A few rules produced that table. Separate projects per environment, so a grant in development cannot reach production. Grant to groups and service accounts, rarely to individuals. Prefer predefined roles over basic ones, and give each workload its own service account. Keep break-glass access rare, logged and reviewed. Then there's evidence. Admin Activity audit logs record configuration changes, such as a policy edit, and are always written. Data Access audit logs, which record reads of data, are off by default for nearly every service, BigQuery being the main exception. So if you need to know who read the order data, you must turn them on, and pay for the volume. Finally, someone has to own the logs, ideally in a project the people being audited cannot change. With identities settled, next we build and run the first application.

The retail application starts with a single job: when someone opens a product page, return that product as JSON. Here's the whole service. It's a small Flask application with one route, slash products slash a sku. Notice there are two moments in this file. The top runs once, when an instance starts up: the imports, creating the app, and reading configuration from the environment. The handler runs once for every request: it looks up the product and returns either the details or a not-found error. That split matters, because anything slow or fragile at start-up delays every request waiting behind it, and anything that fails there stops the instance from serving at all. Next, look at what the code takes from outside. Cloud Run tells the container which port to listen on through the PORT variable, which is 8080 by default, and the production entrypoint binds to it. The bucket name comes from an environment variable that you set on the service, so the same code can run in development and production with different settings. Secrets, such as an API key, should come from Secret Manager when the revision starts, never baked into the image. And dependencies are listed in requirements dot txt and baked into the image when it's built. The bottom card shows the expected behaviour: a known sku returns its name and price, and an unknown one returns a 404 with a short error body. Now we need to turn this folder into something Cloud Run can run.

Cloud Run doesn't run source code. It runs container images, so there's always a build step somewhere. The question is who owns it. The quickest path is a source deploy. You run gcloud run deploy with dash dash source dot, and Cloud Build builds an image for you, using buildpacks to detect a Python app, or your own Dockerfile if the folder has one. The image is stored in Artifact Registry, in a repository called cloud run source deploy, which is created for you in that Region if it doesn't exist. Note that the build runs as an identity of its own, which needs permission to build, and we'll come back to that. The other path is an image deploy. Your own pipeline builds the image, runs tests and scans, pushes it to Artifact Registry with a tag such as one point four point zero, and then you deploy that image. That's more work, but you control the build, its caching and any approval step, which is usually what production wants. Whichever path you take, look at the bottom of the scene. When the revision is created, the tag is resolved to the image's digest, a hash of its exact contents, and the revision keeps that digest. If someone later pushes a different image under the same tag, your running revision doesn't change. So what exactly is a revision?

On Cloud Run, a service is the thing with a stable name and URL: storefront, in europe west 2. What actually runs is a revision. A revision is an immutable snapshot of one image digest plus all its settings: memory, environment variables, the service account, scaling limits. Look at the three revisions in the scene. The first ran version one point three. The second ran one point four. The third runs the same image as the second, and only the memory changed. That still created a new revision, because the settings are part of what a revision is. Old revisions aren't deleted when a new one takes over, and traffic is assigned to revisions by percentage or by tag, which is what lets you send traffic back to one in seconds. Every revision's container has to keep the runtime contract. It must listen on the port in the PORT variable, on all interfaces. A server bound to localhost inside the container can't be reached, and the revision never becomes ready. It must answer each request within the request timeout, five minutes by default and up to sixty. It shouldn't keep state locally: files written to its filesystem live in memory, count against the instance's memory, and disappear when the instance does. And when Cloud Run shuts an instance down, it sends a terminate signal and allows a short grace period to finish up. Next: the identities involved in all this.

Chapter two separated principals, roles and service accounts. Cloud Run is where that pays off, because four identities touch one service. First, the deployer, the person or pipeline creating revisions. They need Cloud Run Developer, and because each revision runs as a service account, they also need permission to act as that account. Without it, the deploy fails even though they can manage the service. Second, for source deploys, the build identity. Cloud Build runs as a service account, the Compute Engine default unless you choose another, and it needs permission to build and push the image. Third, the caller. By default, a Cloud Run service requires the caller to hold Cloud Run Invoker. A public storefront has to be opened deliberately, either by turning off the invoker check, which Google recommends, or by granting the invoker role to all users. Fourth, and most important, is the runtime identity: the service account the code runs as. That's the identity Application Default Credentials finds inside the container, and its roles are the only thing deciding what the code can reach. Here, storefront S A can read objects in one bucket and connect to Cloud SQL, and nothing else. Give each service its own runtime account rather than a broad default. When something is refused, first ask which of the four identities was acting. Next: what happens under load.

Cloud Run scales for you, but it's worth doing the arithmetic yourself. Each instance handles up to eighty concurrent requests by default, and you can raise that to a thousand for code that mostly waits on the network. Suppose the storefront peaks at two thousand four hundred concurrent requests. Divided by eighty, that's thirty instances, comfortably under the default maximum of a hundred. Now the line people forget. If each instance opens a pool of five database connections, the database sees a hundred and fifty connections at peak. Scaling the front end didn't scale the database, and that's usually the first thing to break. Maximum instances is as much a protection for your dependencies as a cap on cost. At the other end, the minimum is zero by default, so an idle service costs nothing. The price is the cold start. A request that arrives when no instance is free waits while one starts: the image is pulled, the container boots, the code imports libraries and opens its connections. That's why start-up work should be lean. Setting minimum instances keeps warm capacity, but you pay for it while it's idle. Billing is a choice too. Request-based billing, the default, charges for CPU only while requests are being handled, so work done after the response may barely run. Instance-based billing charges for the instance's whole lifetime. Next: evidence when things go wrong, and rolling back.

When something fails, the first question is which kind of failure it is. Everything the container writes to standard output or standard error lands in Cloud Logging, tagged with the service and revision. If you write each log line as a JSON object, its fields become structured and searchable. Here, revision four never became ready. The traceback shows the code read an environment variable that wasn't set, and Cloud Run's own message confirms the container never started listening on its port. That's a deployment and configuration failure, not a bug in request handling and not a database outage, and each of those would look different in the logs. Now, releasing. The safer pattern deploys the new version with no traffic and a tag, which gives it its own URL to test. Then you shift a small share of real traffic to it, perhaps ten percent, and watch errors and latency. If they climb, you send all traffic back to the last good revision. That rollback takes seconds, because nothing is rebuilt. The old revision was there all along. But be clear about the limits. Rollback moves traffic. It doesn't undo anything the bad revision wrote. And a timeout is not a rollback either. If the client gives up waiting, the handler may still have finished and written the order, so a blind retry can create a duplicate. Handlers that change data need to be safe to repeat, which we'll return to with events. Next chapter: the network path in front of all this.

Before following a request across Google's network, we need four words. An IP address identifies a machine's network interface. A port identifies a program on that machine, so the storefront listens on one port and a database on another. A protocol, usually TCP or UDP, says how the two sides exchange data. And a CIDR prefix names a whole block of addresses in one short string. Let's work one out. Ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash twenty means the first twenty bits are fixed, and the remaining twelve bits can vary. Two to the power of twelve is four thousand and ninety six addresses, running from ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero to ten dot twenty dot fifteen dot two five five. Google Cloud reserves four addresses in every subnet's primary range: the network address, the default gateway, the second-to-last address and the broadcast address. So four thousand and ninety two are usable. Notice that a smaller number after the slash means a bigger block. Slash sixteen is sixteen times larger than slash twenty. The bottom of the scene shows the three private ranges. They're never routed on the public internet, so every company reuses them. That's exactly why choosing blocks needs care: any two networks you'll ever want to connect must not overlap, and changing addresses later is painful. Next, we use these blocks to build a network.

A VPC network is Google Cloud's private network for your resources, and it has an unusual shape. The network itself is global. One set of routes and firewall rules applies across every Region. Subnets are regional. Each one belongs to a single Region and owns one CIDR range. Here, retail VPC has a subnet in London, ten dot twenty slash twenty, and one in Belgium, ten dot thirty slash twenty. A VM in London can reach a VM in Belgium over internal addresses with no extra setup. Network creation offers two modes. Auto mode creates a subnet in every Region from a fixed block. That's convenient, but those ranges are the same in every auto mode network, so they clash the moment you try to connect two of them. Custom mode makes you choose every range, which is what production should do. So the plan is written down before the first subnet. It leaves ten dot forty free for a future Region, and it never touches one seventy two dot sixteen, which the company's data centre already uses. Subnets can be expanded later but never shrunk, so start modest. Now the contrast this chapter keeps returning to. A global network does not make an application global. It doesn't copy anything anywhere. If every subnet the storefront uses sits in London, the storefront fails with London. Resilience comes from where you choose to run things. Next: how traffic finds its way out.

Every packet that leaves a VM is matched against the network's routes, and the most specific match wins. The route list shows the two kinds every network has. Subnet routes say that anything for ten dot twenty or ten dot thirty stays inside retail VPC. And the default route, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, sends everything else to the default internet gateway. But that gateway only works for a source with an external IP address, and production workloads usually shouldn't have one. So how does an internal-only VM, or a Cloud Run service, call the payments provider? Through Cloud NAT. Cloud NAT is regional, it's configured on a Cloud Router rather than run on a VM, and it translates private source addresses to one or more external ones. Cloud Run joins in through Direct VPC egress, with all its outbound traffic routed into the network, so it leaves through the same NAT. That has a useful side effect. Give the NAT a static address, and the payments provider can allowlist exactly that address. Two limits, though. NAT is outbound only: nothing on the internet can open a connection inward through it. And a route is only a path. Reaching the payments API says nothing about whether your call will be accepted. Next: the rules that decide which traffic is allowed at all.

Routes say where a packet can go. Firewall rules say whether it's allowed. Each rule has a direction, ingress or egress. It has a target, meaning which VMs it applies to, and a source or destination range. Then come the protocols and ports, an action of allow or deny, and a priority. The rule on the left lets Google's load-balancer health checkers, which come from two documented ranges, reach port eighty eighty on the order VMs. It targets them by service account, which is stable and needs IAM to change, unlike an IP address or a network tag that anyone with edit rights can attach. Evaluation runs in order. Hierarchical firewall policies, set on the organisation or folders, are checked first, so a security team can enforce rules that no project can override. Then the network's own rules, lowest priority number first, with deny winning a tie. Finally, if nothing matched, the implied rules at priority sixty five five three five: all ingress denied, all egress allowed. When you can't tell which rule decided, turn on firewall rule logging and read the match. Two facts explain most surprises. First, rules are stateful. If a connection is allowed out, its replies come back without a matching ingress rule. Second, a firewall controls reachability, not identity. A permitted connection still has to pass the application's own authentication and IAM. Next: how names turn into addresses.

Applications don't connect to addresses; they connect to names. So before any packet is routed or filtered, a name has to be resolved. On Google Cloud, a VM sends its DNS queries to the metadata server address, one six nine dot two five four dot one six nine dot two five four, which hands them to Cloud DNS acting as that network's resolver. The resolver consults the zones that network is allowed to see. Cloud DNS has three kinds of zone you'll meet first. A public zone answers anyone on the internet. A private zone answers only the VPC networks you've authorised it for. And a forwarding zone passes queries on, for example to a DNS server in the data centre. Now the failure. The orders database has a private name, orders db dot internal dot retail dot example, in a zone authorised for retail VPC. From a VM in retail VPC, it resolves to ten dot twenty dot four dot five. From a VM in the analytics network, the same query returns NXDOMAIN, meaning no such name. Nothing is broken; the zone simply isn't visible there. The fix is to authorise that network, or to share the zone through DNS peering. The lesson is to read DNS failures for what they are: an answer about visibility from the place you asked. And remember caching: after you change a record, clients keep the old answer until its time to live expires. Check resolution before you blame routes or firewalls. Next: putting a load balancer in front.

Here's the whole storefront path, front to back. A browser looks up shop dot retail dot example. Cloud DNS returns one address, owned by a global external Application Load Balancer. That address is anycast, so users reach the nearest Google edge. The load balancer ends TLS there, using a Google-managed certificate that renews itself, and applies its routing rules. A serverless network endpoint group tells it which Cloud Run service, in which Region, to forward to. The service's ingress setting allows only internal traffic and traffic from the load balancer, so nobody can bypass the front door by calling the run dot app URL directly. Then, on the way out, Direct VPC egress carries the service's database calls to Cloud SQL's private address. Notice that ingress and egress are separate settings. One controls who can reach the service; the other controls how the service reaches others. Neither one is the caller's permission. That's still IAM, or the application's own login. The table is a starting point for choosing a load balancer. Decide the protocol first: HTTP and HTTPS get Application Load Balancers, while other TCP or UDP traffic gets Network Load Balancers. Then decide reach: from the internet or only inside your network, global or regional. An external Application Load Balancer is also where Cloud Armor and Cloud CDN attach. Finally, if the backend must see the client's real address, choose a passthrough balancer. Next: reaching Google's own services privately.

Managed services like Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL don't live inside your VPC network, so how do private workloads reach them without the public internet? Google offers three features with private in their names, and they're easy to confuse. Choose them by purpose. Private Google Access is a subnet setting. It lets VMs that have no external address still reach Google APIs, such as the Cloud Storage API, using Google's API addresses. Private Service Connect creates an endpoint: an internal IP address in your own subnet that stands for a Google API bundle or for a specific published service. Here, ten dot twenty dot nine dot nine stands for a Cloud SQL instance, and you can create such endpoints from several networks, even networks owned by other teams. Private services access works by peering. You allocate an address range, and Google connects your network to a producer network where services like Cloud SQL get their private addresses. Cloud SQL can even offer both private services access and Private Service Connect on one instance, so record which path each workload actually uses. Two things stay the same whichever you choose. A private path grants nothing: the caller still needs IAM permission at the service. And DNS must agree. If the name still resolves to a public address, traffic will try the public route, which may be blocked or may simply not be what you designed. Next: sharing networks across projects and teams.

Chapter one separated projects for ownership and billing. Networking often has to cross those lines, and there are two common patterns. With Shared VPC, there is one network, owned by a host project. The network team manages its subnets, firewall rules and NAT there, in one place. Service projects, such as retail prod and retail analytics, are attached to the host, and their workloads run in subnets they've been granted. App teams deploy without being able to change the network itself. That's usually the right shape inside one organisation: central governance, separate projects. VPC Network Peering is different. Two separate networks, each with its own owner and administration, exchange routes so their workloads can talk over internal addresses. Two rules decide whether it works. Ranges must not overlap, which is why the address plan mattered in section two. And routing is not transitive. Retail VPC is peered with the partner network, and the partner is peered with a third network, but retail still can't reach the third. Each pair needs its own peering. Peering also doesn't merge policies: each side keeps its own firewall rules, and traffic must be allowed on both. It doesn't share private DNS zones either; that needs DNS peering. So choose by ownership. One organisation that wants central control usually picks Shared VPC. Separate owners who need to connect use peering. Next: reaching the company's own data centre.

The retail company's warehouse and fulfilment systems still run in its own data centre, so the VPC network needs a private path there. That's hybrid connectivity, and there are three main options. HA VPN creates encrypted IPsec tunnels over the public internet between a Google gateway and the company's router. It's the fastest to set up, suits modest volumes, and often stays as a backup even after a dedicated link exists. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical circuit between your equipment and Google's, at a colocation facility where both are present. It carries large, steady volumes with more predictable latency. Partner Interconnect gives a similar private path through a service provider, for companies with no presence at one of those facilities. Cross-Cloud Interconnect applies the same idea to another cloud provider. All three share one piece of machinery: Cloud Router. It speaks BGP with the company's router, so each side learns the other's address ranges automatically. When a new subnet is added in Google Cloud, it's advertised to the data centre without anyone editing static routes. Two cautions. First, availability is a design, not a product. HA VPN's service level assumes both tunnels to properly redundant peer equipment, and Interconnect's assumes redundant links, built the way Google documents. Second, Interconnect traffic isn't encrypted by default, so decide whether it must be. With the paths in place, next we compare the places code can run.

So far the storefront has run on Cloud Run, and that was a sensible default. But this chapter steps back and asks a different question. For the orders API, where could it run, and which requirement would actually decide? Start with the workload, not the product. What shape is it? Short requests and responses, a long-running process that holds connections open, or batch jobs that run and finish? How much control do you need? If you need a particular kernel module, a licensed agent installed in the operating system, or a specific GPU, that pushes you towards virtual machines. Do you need portability, for example the same Kubernetes manifests running on-premises too? And can the service tolerate an occasional cold start? The table puts the same API on three platforms. On Compute Engine, you manage the operating system, its patching and its scaling, through managed instance groups. You get full control, and the VMs keep running, and costing, when idle. On GKE, you manage Kubernetes workloads and cluster configuration, which suits many services and teams with Kubernetes skills. On Cloud Run, you manage an image and its settings, and the service can scale to zero. The pattern is consistent: more control means more work that's yours. So choose by the requirement that genuinely can't bend, and revisit the choice when requirements change. Next, a closer look at virtual machines.

A Compute Engine VM is assembled from parts you choose. The machine type sets virtual CPUs and memory: e two standard two is two vCPUs and eight gigabytes. The image is the operating system written onto the boot disk, here the Debian twelve family. From then on, patching that operating system is your job, not Google's. The boot disk is a persistent disk, which is zonal and survives the VM being stopped. The network interface puts it in the app subnet with no external address, and a service account gives the code on it an identity, exactly as chapter two described. The lifecycle has cost consequences people often miss. A running VM is billed for CPU and memory. Stopping it ends those charges, but its disks are still billed, because they still exist. Deleting the VM deletes its boot disk by default, which is convenient for cattle and alarming for a pet you forgot to back up. Finally, access. Instead of copying SSH keys around and giving machines public addresses, turn on OS Login, so IAM decides who may sign in and what they can do, and use Identity-Aware Proxy's TCP forwarding to reach the VM over SSH without any external IP at all. Every sign-in then has an identity and an audit trail. One VM is a start. Next, we manage many of them as a group.

Managing VMs one by one doesn't scale, so Compute Engine separates the recipe from the fleet. An instance template is the recipe: machine type, image, disks, network and service account. Templates are immutable, so a change means a new template, here orders version seven. A managed instance group, or MIG, then keeps a target number of identical VMs running from that template. A regional MIG spreads them across zones in one Region, so if one zone has a problem, only its share of the VMs is affected. Now the distinction that matters most in this section. A MIG responds to two different signals with two different actions. Autoscaling watches load, perhaps CPU utilisation against a target of sixty percent, and changes how many VMs the group should have. Autohealing watches an application health check on each VM, and when one stops answering, it recreates that VM. One adjusts capacity; the other replaces a sick member. They're configured separately and they fail separately. A group can be the right size and still full of broken VMs if there's no health check. Give the health check an initial delay that covers start-up time, or the group will keep recreating VMs that were simply still booting. To change the software, you create a new template and roll it out across the group with a rolling update, which replaces a few VMs at a time so capacity stays up. Next: why asking for more VMs doesn't always work.

Elastic capacity sounds unlimited, but each zone has physical machines, and occasionally a zone doesn't have room for the machine type you asked for. The error on the left came during a sale. The project's quota was fine. The zone simply couldn't fit more of that machine type at that moment. Four terms get mixed up here, and only one of them helps directly. A quota is a limit on how much you're allowed to request. It's not a promise that the capacity exists. A committed use discount is a pricing agreement: commit to one or three years of use and pay less. It doesn't hold any capacity for you. A reservation does. It sets aside capacity for a machine type in one zone, and you pay for it whether or not anything runs in it. And Spot VMs are the opposite trade: spare capacity at a large discount, which Google can reclaim with up to thirty seconds of notice. Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime, but no guarantee either. So design for it. Spread across zones and allow more than one machine type, so a shortage in one place isn't an outage. Reserve only the capacity that must start no matter what, because reservations cost money when idle. And put on Spot only work that can stop and resume safely. Next: what goes into the images these machines run.

Cloud Run, GKE and many VM setups all run container images, so it's worth tracing where an image comes from. The build starts from a base image, which should be pinned, so the same build gives the same result. The image is pushed to Artifact Registry, and from then on it's referred to by its digest, the hash of its exact contents. Artifact Analysis can scan images in the registry and report known vulnerabilities in their operating system packages and language libraries. When the build's checks pass, the pipeline can create an attestation: a signed statement that this digest passed tests and scanning. Binary Authorization can then be set to admit only images carrying the attestations you require, so a hand-built image pushed from someone's laptop simply won't run on GKE or Cloud Run. Now the responsibilities, which are easy to misread. A scan reports; it doesn't patch. Fixing a vulnerable package means rebuilding with an updated base image or dependency, then redeploying. Managed platforms run your image as you built it, so its contents remain your responsibility, even on Cloud Run. Base images and dependencies need regular rebuilds, not just when something breaks. And access to the registry is ordinary IAM: grant read access per repository, to the runtime identities that pull from it, rather than to everyone in the project. Next: Kubernetes, in two modes.

Google Kubernetes Engine runs Kubernetes clusters, and in both of its modes Google operates the control plane, the part that stores cluster state and schedules work. What differs is the nodes, the machines your pods actually run on. In Autopilot mode, Google provisions and manages the nodes. You submit workloads, and you're billed for the CPU and memory your pods request. Look at the requests in the manifest: half a CPU and five hundred and twelve megabytes per replica, times three replicas. Ask for more than you use, and you pay for the difference directly. Autopilot also restricts some node-level settings, because the nodes aren't yours. In Standard mode, you design node pools yourself, choosing machine types and node settings, and you pay for those node VMs whether pods fill them or not. That gives more control, and more ways to waste money if nodes run half empty. Now the part that doesn't change. In both modes, the Deployment, its service account mapping, Kubernetes role-based access, network policies and the timing of upgrades are yours. Managed orchestration still leaves the application and its configuration with you, and you still need people who understand Kubernetes. Compared with Cloud Run, GKE asks for more of that skill in return for more control over how services are deployed, connected and scheduled. Next: the property all three platforms quietly assume.

Every platform in this chapter replaces instances as a matter of routine. Autoscalers remove them when load drops. Autohealing recreates them. Upgrades roll through them. And Spot capacity can be reclaimed at short notice. So code has to expect its instance to disappear. Here's the failure to design against. A fulfilment worker on a Spot VM takes a job: ship order five eight two one three. It inserts a shipment row. Then, before it acknowledges the job as done, its VM is reclaimed. From the queue's point of view the job never finished, so it's delivered again, and a naive worker creates a second shipment. A longer grace period won't fix that, because the interruption can land between any two lines. The real fix is to make the write safe to repeat. Here the shipments table has a unique key on the order, and the insert does nothing if a shipment already exists, so the second attempt changes nothing. Use the notice you do get, too. When the shutdown signal arrives, stop taking new work and finish or hand back what's in flight. The notice is short: up to about thirty seconds for Spot VMs and by default for GKE pods, and ten seconds after Cloud Run's terminate signal. On a VM, a shutdown script can use that window. And keep durable state where it belongs, in databases and storage, never on the instance. Which brings us to storage, next chapter.

The last chapter made instances replaceable on purpose. So anything the retail application must keep, product images, order exports, a VM's database files, has to live somewhere that outlasts the instance. Storage comes in three interfaces, and the interface decides how code uses it. Object storage holds whole files, addressed by a bucket and a name, and read or written over HTTP. That's Cloud Storage, and it suits product images and exports. You don't open an object and edit the middle of it; you read it or replace it. Block storage presents a raw disk that a VM formats with a filesystem. That's Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk, and it suits a database running on a VM, because only that machine writes to it. File storage presents a shared directory over the NFS protocol, which many machines can mount at once. That's Filestore, and here it suits the label printing servers in the warehouse. Now draw the persistence boundary. Buckets, persistent disks and Filestore shares outlive any single instance. A Cloud Run instance's filesystem, which lives in memory, a VM's Local SSD, and anything held in process memory do not. They disappear with the instance. So decide where each piece of state lives before you need it back, not after an instance has gone. Next, Cloud Storage in detail.

Cloud Storage organises data into buckets and objects. A bucket has a name, some settings, and a location that you choose when you create it and can't simply change later. The storefront's images go in a bucket in europe west 2, close to the Cloud Run service that links to them. There are three location types. A Region keeps data in one Region, which gives the lowest latency to compute in that Region. A dual-region keeps data in two named Regions. A multi-region, such as E U, spreads it across a large geographic area. Choose by where the readers are, by any data residency rules, and by what failure you need to tolerate. Then come objects. The copy command uploads a photo as products slash sku one zero four two slash main dot jpg. That looks like folders, but by default the name is one flat string, and the slashes are just characters that tools display as folders. Listing with a prefix finds everything whose name starts with it. If you need real folders, with atomic renames, buckets can be created with a hierarchical namespace. An object is replaced whole: there's no editing a few bytes in the middle. To change the photo, you upload a new one under the same name. And bucket names share one global namespace across all of Google Cloud, which is why the bucket name carries the project's number. Next: who can read and write these objects.

Cloud Storage has two access systems, and new buckets should use only one of them. With uniform bucket-level access turned on, IAM alone decides who can read or write, and the older per-object access lists are switched off. That keeps every grant visible in one place. Now a real flow. A customer wants to attach a photo to a product review. You could stream the upload through the API, but that ties up the service and its memory for no benefit. Instead, the browser asks the API for permission to upload. The API generates a signed URL: valid for one method, PUT, on one object name, for ten minutes. The browser uploads straight to the bucket using that URL, and after ten minutes the URL is useless. Note how the trust works. The URL is signed as the API's own service account, so it can grant no more than that account holds. If the account can't create objects in that bucket, neither can anyone holding the URL. Version four URLs can last up to seven days, but short is safer. Prefer minutes. And the URL can't judge what's uploaded, so check the file's type and size afterwards. Two guard-rails complete the picture. Public access prevention blocks anyone from granting access to all users on the bucket, which stops the classic accidental public bucket. And grant roles on the bucket, choosing the narrowest role, rather than on the whole project. Next: what happens when two writers collide.

Cloud Storage gives a strong promise. Once a write or delete succeeds, every later read and every listing reflects it, anywhere in the world. But strong consistency doesn't prevent lost updates. Look at the scene. The catalogue file is at generation one seven one two. Writer A reads it to change a price. Writer B reads it to change a stock level. A writes generation one seven one three. Then B writes its version, built from the old copy, and A's price change is silently gone. Every write did exactly what it was asked. The fix is a precondition. Every write of an object gets a new generation number. If B writes with if generation match equals one seven one two, Cloud Storage checks first, sees that the generation has moved on, and refuses with four one two, precondition failed. B then re-reads, merges, and tries again. A special value, zero, means create this only if no live object exists, which makes a first write safe to retry. Know where the promise stops, too. Each object is atomic on its own, but there are no transactions across objects: you can't update two objects together, all or nothing. Access-control changes can take time to take effect. And if a public object is served through a cache, readers see the cached copy until its Cache-Control time expires. Next: making storage cheaper, and protecting it.

Every object in Cloud Storage has a storage class, and the classes share one API but price differently. Standard has no minimum duration and no retrieval fee, which suits product images that are read constantly. Nearline, Coldline and Archive store data more cheaply, but charge a fee to read it back, and each has a minimum storage duration: thirty, ninety and three hundred and sixty five days. Delete an Archive object after a month, and you still pay for a year. Lifecycle rules apply these classes automatically. The order exports, for instance, can move to Coldline after ninety days and be deleted after seven years, with no code to maintain. Now, protection, because someone will eventually delete the wrong file. Object Versioning keeps an overwritten or deleted object as a noncurrent version, so the previous content can be restored. Soft delete keeps deleted objects restorable for a retention window, seven days by default, configurable up to ninety. A retention policy goes further and refuses deletion until each object reaches a set age, and it can be locked so even administrators can't shorten it. An object hold pins individual objects, for example while legal reviews them. Each costs something: versions and soft-deleted objects are billed as storage. So choose the protection each bucket needs, rather than all of it everywhere. Next: disks.

Virtual machines need block storage for their filesystems, and Google Cloud offers several kinds. Persistent Disk is the long-standing option. Its performance grows with its size, so a small disk is also a slow disk. It can be zonal, or regional, where writes are replicated synchronously to a second zone in the same Region. Hyperdisk is the newer family. With Hyperdisk Balanced, you provision IOPS and throughput separately from capacity, so a small, busy database doesn't have to buy terabytes it doesn't need just to go faster. It attaches only to supported machine types, so check before choosing. Local SSD is physically attached to the host and very fast, which makes it tempting. But it doesn't persist: its data is lost when the VM stops or is moved. Use it only for caches and scratch space you can rebuild. Then there's file storage. Filestore is managed NFS, mounted by many clients at once. The warehouse label servers all read the same templates from one share, and its service tier sets performance and availability. Two rules help in choosing. If many machines need to write the same files, use a file service; don't try to share one block disk between them. And a regional disk survives the loss of a zone, but it faithfully replicates every write, including a bad one. Which is exactly the subject of the next section.

This chapter closes on the distinction people most often get wrong. Replication keeps copies in step. That protects you from losing a copy, a disk, a zone. But it copies mistakes just as faithfully. Follow the incident. At two in the morning, a scheduled snapshot of the stock disk runs. Snapshots are incremental, so each one stores only what changed. At nine fourteen, a bad deploy overwrites stock levels with zeros. The disk is regional, so within seconds both zones hold the wrong data. Replication did its job perfectly, and it doesn't help at all. Only a copy taken before nine fourteen can get the data back, and the newest one is the two o'clock snapshot. The restore is careful. Create a new disk from the snapshot, beside the damaged one, never over it, because you might need the damaged disk to recover later changes. Attach it to a test machine and check row counts and totals against what you expect. Then decide. Any changes made between two and nine fourteen are either replayed from another source, such as the order events, or accepted as lost. That gap is the recovery point. And the last claim on the slide is the one to remember. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Restore drills, timed and checked, are the evidence. And keep backups apart from what they protect, in another project or Region, with different administrators, so one mistake or one compromised account can't reach both. Next chapter: databases.

Cloud Storage keeps bytes safe, but it can't answer a question like: which orders for this customer are unpaid? That's a database's job, and different databases are good at different questions. So this chapter starts with the data, not with products. Look at the retail application's data in the table. Orders and payments involve several rows that must change together, all or nothing, and they're queried with joins. That calls for transactions, so the starting point is Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The product catalogue is read far more than it's written, usually one product at a time by its id, and its shape varies by category. Firestore fits that well. Sessions and hot reads need speed more than durability, which is a cache's job, Memorystore. Click events arrive at a huge rate, keyed by customer, which is where Bigtable could come in if volumes grow. And if stock were ever written in many Regions at once without overselling, Spanner would be the answer. Note those last two are introduced by specific requirements, not because a database has grown. Most growing databases need indexes, replicas or caches long before they need a different engine. One more principle: ownership. Each dataset should belong to one service. Other services ask that service through its API, rather than reading its tables directly, so schemas can change without breaking strangers. Next: Cloud SQL itself.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is PostgreSQL that Google operates. Google provisions the machine and storage, applies patches during a maintenance window you choose, takes automated backups, keeps the transaction logs needed for point-in-time recovery, and, if you turn on high availability, fails over to a standby. That removes a lot of operational work. But look at the right-hand column, because it's what managed services can't do for you. The schema and its indexes are yours, and a missing index makes the most powerful instance slow. The queries are yours. Connections are yours: how many each application instance opens, and how many the database allows. And the users and grants inside PostgreSQL are yours. IAM decides who may connect to the instance; PostgreSQL's own permissions decide which tables they can read. AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is the other managed PostgreSQL option. It's compatible with PostgreSQL, so the skills and most of the code carry over, but its architecture is different. Storage is scaled separately from compute, and a columnar engine speeds up analytical scans over operational data. It's worth evaluating when a busy Cloud SQL instance is genuinely the limit, or when the same database must serve heavy reporting queries alongside transactions. For the retail orders database, Cloud SQL is the sensible starting point. Next: what a transaction looks like, and how the API connects.

Here's the heart of the orders service. Placing an order changes three tables: it reduces stock, inserts the order, and inserts its line. Wrapped in BEGIN and COMMIT, those three statements form one transaction. The stock update only matches a row if at least one item is on hand, so if the shirt sold out a moment ago, zero rows change and the service stops before inserting anything. If anything fails before COMMIT, PostgreSQL discards all of it, and no half-placed order ever exists. That's the guarantee that made us choose a relational database. Now the failure that usually arrives first in production, and it isn't the database running out of CPU. It's connections. Remember the arithmetic from Cloud Run. During a sale, thirty instances each open a pool of ten connections. That's three hundred, more than this instance is configured to accept, and PostgreSQL replies: sorry, too many clients already. Requests fail even though the database is barely busy. The fixes are smaller pools per instance, a connection pooler in front of the database, or a maximum instance count that fits what the database can take. And connect safely. Cloud SQL's connectors, the Auth Proxy or a language library, handle encryption and authorisation, and IAM database authentication lets the service sign in as its own service account, with no password stored anywhere. Next: keeping the database available.

Four Cloud SQL features each involve another copy of the database, which is why they're so often confused. Each one answers a different failure. High availability keeps a standby instance in a second zone. If the primary or its zone fails, Cloud SQL fails over to the standby, usually within a minute or so, and the application reconnects. It doesn't add read capacity, and it faithfully keeps a bad write. Read replicas are asynchronous copies that take read traffic off the primary. They help with read load, but they don't promise fresh data. Backups with point-in-time recovery let you create a new instance as it was at a chosen moment, such as one second before a bad migration. That undoes mistakes, but it takes time and creates a new instance. And a maintenance window lets you choose when the occasional restart for patching happens. It doesn't remove the restart. Now look at the card. A customer pays. The primary commits the status change at noon exactly. A hundred and fifty milliseconds later, the order page reads from a replica and still sees placed, because the replica hasn't applied the change yet. Nearly two seconds pass before it catches up. The customer thinks the payment failed. The rule: reads that must see your own write go to the primary. Next: a database of documents instead of tables.

Firestore stores documents, which look like JSON objects, grouped into collections. The product catalogue fits it well. Each product is a document such as products slash sku one zero four two. It's read whole and almost always by its id, and its fields vary: shirts have sizes, but gift cards don't. Every field gets a single-field index automatically, so simple queries just work. Now look at the second card. The storefront asks for shirts, ordered by price. That filters on one field and sorts by another, which needs a composite index, and Firestore refuses the query until one exists. The error even includes a link to create it. In a real project, declare composite indexes in configuration and deploy them with the code, so the next environment doesn't fail the same way. Firestore has transactions too. Inside one, you read documents and then write them, and the whole thing commits atomically or retries. What it doesn't have is joins. If a page needs a product and its category's banner, either read two documents or copy the banner into the product. Shape documents for the reads you make. Two cautions. Firestore runs in Native mode or Datastore mode, and they differ in features and behaviour, so check which one you're reading about. And don't move the orders here just to avoid SQL. Next: when even PostgreSQL isn't enough.

Sooner or later someone asks: shouldn't we just use Spanner? So it's worth being precise about what it's for. Spanner is a relational database with SQL, schemas and transactions, but unlike a single PostgreSQL primary, it scales out. Data is split across many servers, and the database keeps transactions strongly consistent across all of them. It goes further, offering what Google calls external consistency: if one transaction commits before another starts, everyone sees them in that order, as if the whole database were one machine. It runs in regional configurations, with replicas across zones, or multi-region configurations that survive the loss of a Region. That power has costs. The minimum price is higher than a small Cloud SQL instance. Multi-region writes have to reach replicas further apart, so they take longer. And schema and key design need care, because a badly chosen key concentrates load. So look at the decision table for the retail stock data. If the shop runs in one Region and takes a few thousand orders a minute, Cloud SQL is enough. If the load is mostly reads, replicas or a cache will help more. Only if stock is written in many Regions at once, and must never be oversold, does Spanner earn its cost. It's an answer to a requirement, not the next stage every database grows into. Next: a very different large-scale database.

Bigtable is built for a different kind of scale: tables with billions of rows, taking very high rates of reads and writes, but with simple access. Rows are stored sorted by their row key, and the key is the only index. So designing the key is designing the database. Look at the first set of keys for click events. Each one starts with a timestamp. Since time only moves forward, every new write lands at the end of the key range, which is served by one part of the cluster. That's a hot spot: one node works flat out while the rest wait, and adding nodes doesn't help. The second design starts with the customer id, then the time. Writes from different customers now spread across the whole key range, and as a bonus, one customer's events sit together, so reading a customer's recent activity is a single short scan. A few more facts set expectations. Changes to a single row are atomic, but there are no transactions across rows. Throughput grows as you add nodes, but only if the keys spread the load. And there are no joins: you design keys for the scans you'll actually run. Bigtable fits click streams, time series and huge keyed lookups. It's not a replacement for the orders database. The retail app would only reach for it if click volume truly demanded it. Next: caches, and moving databases.

The last tool in this chapter makes reads fast by keeping a second copy. Memorystore is a managed in-memory store, compatible with Redis and Valkey, and the storefront uses it in the cache-aside pattern. On a read, check the cache first. If the product's there, return it in a millisecond. If not, read the database, store the result in the cache with a time to live, and return it. Now follow the timeline. At nine o'clock, the linen shirt is cached at thirty nine pounds, with a ten-minute time to live. At two minutes past, the price drops to twenty nine pounds in the database. For the next eight minutes, the cache keeps serving the old price, because nothing told it otherwise. The fix is to delete the cached key whenever the product is written, so the next read refreshes it, and keep the time to live as a safety net in case a delete is missed. The same question, which copy is true, governs moving a database. A migration copies all the data to the target, then replicates ongoing changes until the target catches up. At cutover, writes stop briefly, the remaining lag drains, and connections switch to the target. Database Migration Service can manage much of this for PostgreSQL. And decide the way back before you start, because during an incident is the worst time to design one. Next chapter: events and workflows.

So far, the storefront and orders API have served the retail company's own pages. Now partners, such as a marketplace that resells the shirts, want to check order status from their systems. That's the moment to put a gateway in front of the API. A gateway enforces a contract before any request reaches the backend. The contract here is an OpenAPI document: it lists the paths and methods that exist, says callers must present an API key, and names the Cloud Run backend. The gateway rejects unknown paths, identifies the caller from its key or a signed token, and applies a quota per caller, so one noisy partner can't exhaust the service for everyone. Google Cloud offers two gateways, and the choice is about scope. API Gateway is a simple managed gateway, designed for serverless backends like Cloud Run. You give it a spec, and it routes, authenticates and limits. Apigee is a full API management platform. It adds a policy engine for transforming and protecting traffic, API products that bundle endpoints for different partners, a developer portal, and detailed analytics. If you're publishing one API to a few partners, API Gateway fits. If you're running an API programme, with many products, partners and policies, Apigee does. One thing stays with the backend either way: deciding whether this particular partner may see this particular order. Next: small pieces of code that react to events.

Some work doesn't need a whole service. When a product photo is uploaded, the storefront needs thumbnails, and that's a few lines of code that should run whenever an image arrives. Cloud Run functions is built for exactly that. You write a single handler, Google builds it into a container, and it runs on Cloud Run underneath. It can answer HTTP requests, or react to events. Here's the flow. An image is written to the products bucket, and Cloud Storage emits an object finalized event. An Eventarc trigger matches events of that type from that bucket and calls the function. The handler receives a CloudEvent, reads the bucket, the object name and its generation, ignores anything outside the products prefix, and makes the thumbnail. Because it runs on Cloud Run, everything from chapter three still applies. Each run has a timeout. Nothing in memory or on local disk survives between events. And the same event can be delivered more than once, so writing the thumbnail must be safe to repeat. Here, it's keyed by the source object's generation, so a second run produces the same result. One trap is worth naming. If the thumbnails were written back into the same prefix the trigger watches, each thumbnail would trigger another run, and the function would chase its own tail. Finally, give the function its own service account, with only what it needs. Next: the messaging service underneath many of these flows.

When an order is placed, several parts of the business need to know: fulfilment must ship it, the customer needs an email, and the analytics team wants it in their warehouse. The orders API could call each of them, but then it would need to know them all, and fail when any of them failed. Pub/Sub separates the two sides. The orders API publishes one message, order placed, to a topic. It doesn't know who's listening. Listeners attach subscriptions to the topic, and each subscription receives every message, with its own independent delivery state. There are several kinds. The fulfilment subscription is pull: worker processes ask for messages, process them and acknowledge each one. The email subscription is push: Pub/Sub makes an HTTPS request to the email service for each message. The analytics subscription writes straight into a BigQuery table, and the archive subscription batches messages into files in Cloud Storage, with no code at all. This shape buys three things. A new consumer can join by adding a subscription, without touching the publisher. A slow consumer delays only its own subscription, so a backlog in email doesn't slow fulfilment. And if a consumer is down, its messages wait, up to the subscription's retention period, rather than being lost. Note what a successful publish means: the message is stored, not that anyone has processed it yet. Next: exactly what happens to one message on one subscription.

Let's follow one message through one subscription. Pub/Sub delivers it to a worker, and the acknowledgement deadline starts, ten seconds by default and extendable up to ten minutes. The worker does its job and acknowledges the message, and Pub/Sub removes it from that subscription. That's the happy path. Now suppose the acknowledgement doesn't arrive in time, because the worker crashed, was slow, or the ack was lost on the network. Pub/Sub assumes the message wasn't handled and delivers it again, possibly to a different worker. A worker that knows it can't finish can nack the message, asking for redelivery straight away. That's what at-least-once delivery means, and it's why every consumer must expect duplicates. Two features change the guarantees, each with clear limits. Ordering keys: messages published with the same key, such as the order id, are delivered in the order they were published, as long as they were published to the same region. There's no ordering across different keys, and one slow key holds up the messages queued behind it. Exactly-once delivery is a subscription setting for pull subscriptions, within a region. It guarantees that once a message has been successfully acknowledged, it won't be redelivered. Read that boundary carefully. It doesn't stop a publisher from publishing the same order twice after a retry, and it can't make your database write and your acknowledgement a single atomic act. Next: routing events from Google services themselves.

Eventarc is the router between event sources and the services that react to them. Sources include Google services like Cloud Storage, events derived from Cloud Audit Logs, such as someone changing an IAM policy, and your own Pub/Sub topics. Destinations include Cloud Run services and functions, Workflows, and services on GKE. Events arrive in a standard envelope called a CloudEvent. A trigger ties the two together, and the command on the left shows its three parts. Filters say which events match: here, object finalized events, from one bucket only. The destination is the thumbnailer service. And the trigger acts as a service account. That last part is where most first attempts fail silently. To deliver an event, the trigger's service account has to call the destination, so it needs the Cloud Run Invoker role on that service. If it doesn't have it, the trigger is created anyway, looks perfectly healthy, and delivers nothing. Grant the role on the one destination service, not across the whole project. One more caution. Some sources only reach Eventarc through audit logs, and some of those log types, Data Access logs in particular, are off by default, as chapter two noted. If the audit log isn't written, there's no event to route. Next: two services that are easy to confuse.

Cloud Tasks and Pub/Sub both move work off the request path, so they're often confused. Google's own framing is the clearest: implicit versus explicit invocation. Look at the two jobs that follow an order. The first is announcing that an order was placed. The orders service doesn't know, and shouldn't know, everyone who cares. That's an event, and Pub/Sub distributes it. Subscribers decide to listen, any number of them, and each consumer controls its own rate through flow control. The second job is booking a pickup with the carrier. That's a specific call to one specific target, and the carrier's API allows only five requests a second. That's dispatch, and Cloud Tasks fits. Each task names its target, an HTTP endpoint or service. The queue sets how fast tasks are dispatched and how failures are retried, so the carrier is never flooded. Tasks can be scheduled for later, for example to book the pickup at eight tomorrow morning. And a task can be given a name, so creating the same task twice is rejected, which removes a whole class of duplicates at the source. So ask: am I announcing something that happened, or asking one particular service to do one particular thing? Announcements go to Pub/Sub. Requests go to Cloud Tasks. Either way, both retry, so both targets must be safe to repeat. Next: when a process needs several steps, in order.

Fulfilling an order takes three calls to three services, in order: reserve the stock, take the payment, book the shipping. Chaining those calls inside one request handler is fragile. If the handler dies after the first call, nobody knows where things stand. Workflows is a managed orchestrator for exactly this. You describe the steps in YAML, and Workflows runs them, keeping the state between steps durably, so a long process survives restarts. Each step here calls a service over HTTP, authenticated as the workflow's own service account. The charge step has a retry policy, so a brief payment outage is retried automatically. And it has an except block, which runs if the charge finally fails. That block is the important idea in this section: compensation. The stock was already reserved. There's no database transaction spanning three services that could roll it back.
